title: India's First High-Altitude Snow Leopard Safari Flags Off in Ladakh
excerpt: Six open-back safari vehicles rolled out of Leh during Wildlife Week for India's first high-altitude wildlife safari, initially covering Rumbak, Shang and Uley with trained local guides.
body:
• Ladakh has launched what the administration describes as India's first high-altitude wildlife safari: six specially designed open-back vehicles were flagged off in Leh on Oct. 7 by Lt. Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena during Wildlife Week celebrations, about two months after the plan was approved.
  • The safari will initially operate in Rumbak, Shang and Uley, with trained local drivers and wildlife guides taking visitors through designated areas in search of snow leopards — alongside Himalayan brown bears, wolves and more than 340 bird species.
  • What it means for you: The classic sighting window is January to March, per the Snow Leopard Conservancy India Trust's visitor guidance. Plan at least 48 hours of acclimatization in Leh — a Ladakh Tourism advisory requirement — and book only through a registered local travel company with an experienced local naturalist or guide, as Ladakh's wildlife-tour rules require. The administration has not yet published a tariff or booking portal for the new safari, and no sighting is ever guaranteed: more field days improve the odds, not the certainty.
  • Ladakh hosts 477 of India's estimated 718 snow leopards, the country's largest population. Authorities plan to extend routes across Hemis National Park, Changthang, Karakoram Wildlife Sanctuary, Nubra, Zanskar, Sham, Kargil and Drass — and also inaugurated an AI-based device for preventing human-wildlife conflict.

Six specially designed open-back vehicles rolled out of Leh on Wednesday, flagging off India's first high-altitude wildlife safari — a state-run programme giving tourists a regulated, guided shot at spotting the snow leopard in Ladakh's wilds.

Announced by Lt. Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena in a post on X, the flag-off took place during Wildlife Week celebrations in Leh, roughly two months after the administration approved the initiative, according to the Hindu BusinessLine.

From approval to flag-off

The groundwork was laid on Aug. 6, when Saxena approved the country's first high-altitude wildlife safari at the first governing body meeting of the newly constituted Snow Leopard and High-Altitude Nature (SHAN) Conservation Society. The Forest Department was directed to introduce guided jeep safaris on the lines of popular parks like Kaziranga and Ranthambore.

The administration says the programme fuses tourism, conservation and local livelihoods: twenty local youths will be trained in birdwatching and equipped with binoculars, ten birdwatching hides will be created at major hotspots, and communities are to be partners in protecting wildlife — and earn from wildlife tourism — rather than treating conservation and tourism separately. Authorities also inaugurated an AI-based device for preventing human-wildlife conflict, described as the first of its kind.

Why Ladakh, why the cat

Ladakh is the natural home for this: the Wildlife Institute of India's first national assessment estimated 718 snow leopards across India — 477 in Ladakh. The region also supports 38+ mammal species, 340+ bird species and around 1,800 vascular plant species, and visitors may see Himalayan brown bears and wolves.

Snow leopards rank among the most difficult animals to spot: they live in remote, rocky high-altitude terrain and stay largely hidden from people. Ladakh's snow-leopard tracking recently made a global top-5 wildlife-experiences list, putting the region's rare encounters firmly on the international travel map.

Experts question the jeep model

The open-jeep format has drawn skeptical questions. Outlook Traveller spoke to MK Ranjitsinh Jhala — India's first Director of Wildlife Preservation, author of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 — and Lobzang Visuddha of Leh's Wildlife Tour Operators Association. Both welcomed communities earning more from wildlife tourism; neither was convinced the open-jeep model, borrowed from lowland parks, fits how snow leopard tracking actually works in Ladakh — long, patient scanning from ridgelines with spotting scopes. The administration says the guided system should also curb illegal off-roading and wildlife disturbance.

Planning your trip

A dedicated snow leopard trip is a winter expedition. The Snow Leopard Conservancy India Trust identifies January to March as the best sighting period, when the cats descend to lower altitudes; commercial operators typically run departures from November to March. Planners recommend around nine to eleven days in Ladakh, including acclimatization and several full search days.

Altitude is the first hurdle, not the cold: Ladakh Tourism's advisory calls for at least 48 hours of rest in Leh after arrival, and altitude sickness is common among fly-in visitors. Pack warm layers, insulated footwear, binoculars, spare batteries — cold drains them fast — and sun protection. Under Ladakh's wildlife-tour rules, trips must run through a registered local travel company with an experienced local naturalist or guide, and no final route map, booking portal or tariff has been published yet — so confirm operating status and pricing before committing.

What's next

Authorities say more routes will follow across Hemis National Park, Changthang, Karakoram, Nubra, Zanskar, Sham, Kargil and Drass. For diaspora travellers who already route India trips through Leh, the safari adds a new winter anchor beyond the monasteries and road trips — and a reason to schedule for January-March rather than summer. The coming winter season will be the real test of whether the jeep-safari model and the conservation pitch hold together.
